candidates.attacker_control: An authenticated/authorized NiFi user who can create or configure Controller Services (or a processor that references the service) controls the values evaluated into the JNDI environment in JndiJmsConnectionFactoryHandler.createInitialContext(): `java.naming.factory.initial` (JNDI Initial Context Factory Class), `java.naming.provider.url` (JNDI Provider URL, expression-language capable via variable registry), `connection.factory.name` (lookup name, passed verbatim to InitialContext.lookup()), the JNDI / JMS Client Libraries classpath entries, and arbitrary dynamic properties that are copied into the JNDI environment (lines 125-129). All are attacker-chosen strings that reach JDK JNDI APIs.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether a stronger guard exists elsewhere: `connection.factory.name` uses only NON_EMPTY_VALIDATOR (JndiJmsConnectionFactoryProperties.java:62-69) and is passed unfiltered to lookup(); `java.naming.factory.initial` uses only NON_EMPTY_VALIDATOR; dynamic properties are copied into the JNDI environment with VALID-only validation. Checked the documented intent in additionalDetails.html (104-119), which lists the exact allowed schemes and the override property, so the substring acceptance is not a documented feature. Checked that the `instanceof ConnectionFactory` check (JndiJmsConnectionFactoryHandler.java:98-101) happens after lookup() and therefore is not a pre-deserialization guard. Noted: the classic dangerous spellings "ldap", "ldaps", "rmi", "iiop", "dns" are NOT substrings of the allow-listed schemes, so a *direct* provider-URL bypass with those literals is blocked; the concrete exploit primitive therefore additionally relies on the accept-by-default branch (inputs not matching the "scheme://..." pattern), on the attacker-selected initial context factory behavior for substring schemes, or on the separately unvalidated lookup name — this uncertainty is why the finding is submitted as a source-evidence lead, not a confirmed exploit.
candidates.impact: Defeat of the JNDI provider-URL restriction intended to prevent untrusted remote JNDI resolution. Where a reachable remote provider (e.g. LDAP/RMI-style naming service, or another scheme accepted by the configured initial context factory) can be reached, the NiFi host may deserialize objects returned by that service, which is a well-known path to remote code execution under the NiFi process account; at minimum it enables SSRF to arbitrary naming-service endpoints, credential exposure (JNDI environment including principal/credentials is sent to the attacker-chosen provider), and disclosure of class/type information.
candidates.prerequisites: A user able to configure the JNDI JMS Connection Factory service (or a processor providing attribute values used by its variable-registry expression language), plus reachability from the NiFi host to an attacker-controlled JNDI/LDAP/RMI endpoint. The service must be enabled so that lookupConnectionFactory() runs. Exact exploitability of a given bypass spelling depends on the configured initial context factory and on JDK JNDI URL/provider parsing, which was not runtime-verified here.
candidates.root_cause: JndiJmsProviderUrlValidator.isSchemeAllowed() iterates the allowed set and tests `allowedScheme.contains(scheme)` instead of `allowedSchemes.contains(scheme)` (equality), so any scheme that is a substring of an allowed scheme (e.g. "t", "s", "t3", "sl", "ud", "file", "jgroups", "vm") passes validation. In addition, isUrlAllowed() returns `allowed = true` whenever the regex `^([^:]+)://.+$` does not match, so provider URLs that omit the "//" form (and other non-matching spellings) are never scheme-checked. The documented contract (additionalDetails.html lines 104-119) and the property description state that only the exact schemes file/jgroups/ssl/t3/t3s/tcp/udp/vm are allowed, and the Java system property override is documented as a space-separated list of schemes, so the code contradicts its own specification.
candidates.title: Ineffective JNDI provider URL scheme allow-list in JndiJmsConnectionFactoryProvider (substring comparison, plus accept-by-default for non-URL inputs) enables unsafe remote JNDI resolution/deserialization
candidates.trace: 1) PropertyDescriptor JNDI_PROVIDER_URL (JndiJmsConnectionFactoryProperties.java:53-60) is `required(true)`, expression-language scoped, and validated only by JndiJmsProviderUrlValidator. 2) validate() (lines 157-174) delegates to isUrlAllowed() (176-188): if `^([^:]+)://.+$` matches, the captured scheme goes to isSchemeAllowed() (190-201), which accepts when any allow-listed entry *contains* the supplied scheme; if the regex does not match, the URL is accepted with no scheme check. 3) At runtime, JndiJmsConnectionFactoryHandler.createInitialContext() (110-135) copies the attacker-controlled `java.naming.provider.url`, `java.naming.factory.initial`, principal/credentials and every dynamic property into a Hashtable and instantiates `new InitialContext(env)` (line 133) — i.e. an attacker-selected JNDI provider/factory is honored. 4) lookupConnectionFactory() (85-107) calls `initialContext.lookup(factoryName)` (line 91) with the attacker-controlled connection-factory name; only after the lookup returns is the `instanceof ConnectionFactory` check applied (98-101), so any deserialization/object-return side effects of the lookup occur before validation. 5) Result: the allow-list that is supposed to keep remote/untrusted JNDI providers out of reach can be bypassed with accepted spellings, allowing the service to contact an attacker-controlled naming/directory service and to resolve/deserialize objects it returns.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no JDK/JNDI behavior was run; the exact bypass string that provably causes remote resolution for a given JDK version and configured context factory was not determined. Whether the substring comparison is an upstream defect or a deliberately modified line cannot be established from the snapshot alone (no VCS history available in this run). Also unverified: whether NiFi's framework-level authorization/policy checks meaningfully limit who can set these properties beyond the documented 'authenticated and authorized user' assumption.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization / CWE-184 Incomplete List of Disallowed Inputs (improper restriction of JNDI provider URL)

coverage_summary: Review was targeted rather than exhaustive: full line-level reading of the JMS bundle JNDI path (JndiJmsConnectionFactoryProperties.java, JndiJmsConnectionFactoryProvider.java, JndiJmsConnectionFactoryHandler.java, provider documentation), plus broad literal searches across all readable files for high-risk sink families (ObjectInputStream, InitialContext/JNDI lookups, deserialization entry points) and directory/structure reconnaissance of the ~8256-file NiFi 1.22.0 tree. The P1 relation index covers 7984 of 8256 source files (272 missing from the index), is 'partial', has only syntax containment plus name/type/arity call candidates (control flow, data flow and semantic resolution 'not_implemented', 165551 unresolved calls, 3 parse errors, 249 omitted files), and index facts are name-based navigation hints only; no relation-index edge was treated as proof. Large parts of the repository (nifi-framework, nifi-web, standard processors, DBCP/JMS providers beyond the JNDI path, MiNiFi/C2 modules) were not read and are not claimed as reviewed.
limitations: No build, tests, or code execution were performed; all impact reasoning (JNDI provider/URL parsing, deserialization, RCE) is static and unconfirmed.

The relation index does not implement control flow, data flow, or semantic resolution and has unresolved/omitted files, so absence of an index edge for a code path is not evidence that the path does not exist.

JDK-internal behavior (InitialContext provider parsing, scheme-to-URL-context-factory resolution, whether a substring scheme or a non-'://' provider URL results in remote resolution) could not be checked against JDK sources in this run.
No VCS history or patch data is available, so it cannot be determined whether the substring comparison is the original upstream code or an introduced modification.
Only the JMS JNDI area was reviewed in depth; other plausible surfaces (DBCP/H2 JDBC URL, web/UI endpoints, other processors' path/URL handling) remain uninspected.

summary: Apache NiFi 1.22.0 source snapshot (8256 files, ~6500 Java files). The strongest source-supported candidate is in the JMS JNDI Connection Factory support: `JndiJmsProviderUrlValidator` is intended (and documented) to limit the JNDI provider URL to an explicit scheme allow-list, but its scheme test is implemented as `allowedScheme.contains(scheme)`, i.e. the input scheme is accepted whenever it is a *substring* of any allowed scheme (and any input not matching `^([^:]+)://.+$` is accepted outright). This makes the mitigation ineffective, and JNDI lookup of an attacker-supplied name is then performed with an attacker-controlled initial-context factory class and attacker-controlled JNDI environment/dynamic properties, with the `instanceof ConnectionFactory` check occurring only after the (potentially remote, deserializing) `lookup()` call. No runtime confirmation was performed; impact reasoning is based on JDK JNDI semantics and must be treated as a lead.
